item.title: NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B
item.abstract: NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma , a collection of 14 open checkpoints at 3B and 8B scale. Nemotron-Labs-Sigma is a continuous diffusion language model family that denoises text in a 16-D embedding space. Most diffusion LLMs, such as LLaDA and Dream, work on discrete tokens. Sigma works in a smooth latent space instead. NVIDIA team states that this makes few-step distillation and trajectory steering practical for text. The research team calls Sigma the first large-scale family of continuous diffusion language models. The collection has 4 variant types at each size: Each token maps to a point in a learned 16-D embedding space . Training adds Gaussian noise to these embeddings and teaches the model to remove it. The embedding geometry is learned jointly with the denoiser. Generation runs blockwise. Each denoised block is committed to a KV cache before the next starts. Blocks default to 64 tokens. The backbone is a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention, SwiGLU and rotary embeddings. Training starts from an autoregressive warm start of about 1T tokens. About 0.3T tokens of diffusion training follow. At inference, classifier-free guidance and score temperature matter most. The model card page recommends guidance 3 and temperature 0.3 at 32 DDIM steps. Discrete diffusion jumps between token states, so its trajectories are hard to steer. Sigma follows smooth ODE/SDE paths instead. Per the research paper , these degrade gracefully at low step counts and distill efficiently. Embedding-space steering also tunes the quality-diversity trade-off for pass@k sampling. On the research’s 6-task base suite, Sigma-8B with 256 DDPM steps averages 71.16. NLD-8B in diffusion mode scores 70.22, Dream-7B 58.74 and LLaDA-8B 41.78. Qwen3-8B in AR mode scores 68.91. A cheaper 32-step DDIM sampler still gives Sigma-8B a 70.18 average. Coding is the standout. Sigma-8B scores 65.12 on HumanEval versus 62.80 for NLD-8B. MBPP is weaker, at 65.74 versus 67.00. After SFT, Sigma-8B-instruct scores 91.96 on GSM8K, 78.40 on MATH-500 and 82.50 on HumanEval. Hard reasoning stays limited, at 23.33 on AIME24 and 17.00 on AIME25. Its 10-task average of 59.14 sits just below NLD-8B at 59.92. All scores are NVIDIA’s own evaluations. Sigma-distill-8B-nfe8 decodes each 32-token block in 8 denoiser calls plus 1 readout. Its card reports a 6-task mean of 70.34, with 88.44 on GSM8K and 65.18 on HumanEval. That is close to the 256-step teacher. NVIDIA’s launch thread frames the gain as 8 tokens per forward on math and 4 on code. The distill-spec checkpoints add self-speculative decoding. A diffusion head drafts a 32-token block, and the model’s own AR head verifies it. Output exactly matches greedy AR decoding. On 1 GB200 with SGLang, the 8B spec model runs 3.46x faster than AR decoding on average. NLD-8B reaches 3.04x on the same setup. Peak speedups reach 4.20x at 8B and 3.18x at 3B. All 14 checkpoints are on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License. The cards state the models are ready for commercial use. You need a CUDA GPU in bfloat16: Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper or Blackwell. CPU inference is not supported. Loading needs PyTorch 2.4+, Transformers 4.55+ and trust_remote_code . On 1 H100, the base model generates about 120 to 140 tokens/s. The distilled card lists vLLM, SGLang and Docker Model Runner for serving. NVIDIA hosts no API. Benchmark rows use NVIDIA’s evaluations from the Sigma paper (Table 2 base, Table 5 instruct). Specs come from each model’s own card. Check out the Paper , Model Collection and Project Page . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
item.abstract:
Abstract In our previous post, Redwood , we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?” Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core. Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts. Introduction to interaction nets Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly. Interaction nets 1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine 2 compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3 Fig. 1. Five queens, two ways. On the left, a C++ program walks the search tree one step at a time. On the right, the same search as an interaction net explores many branches at once: 3,183 interactions with a critical path of only 262 steps. Fig. 1 shows the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away. In theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent. Process Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way. Fig. 2. The Frostbite program from first proposal to ablations: key events, the stages of work, and the worktrees the agents created, with each branch drawn in its phase's color. Architecture exploration and selection To begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work. Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression. Fig. 3. All 25 workloads, grouped by how each program exposes its work, and split into the search set the agents tuned on and the held-out eval set, with the size each was run at. Agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible. Formal contracts and system modeling Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.” In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team.

item.title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
item.abstract: Back to Articles Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Published November 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 25 +19 Younes B ybelkada Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Nathan Habib SaylorTwift Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Amine Dirhoussi aminediroHF Follow Adithya S K AdithyaSK Follow shaun smith evalstate Follow Sergio Paniego sergiopaniego Follow Joel Niklaus joelniklaus Follow Lewis Tunstall lewtun Follow Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. TL;DR We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself. Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , OpenEnv and harbor. Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode. All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection . Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Testing the filters with short training runs AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Final results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Training inside agent harnesses We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer. Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv . We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains. RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything. This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate , and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B. Three sources Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves: SWE-smith ( Python , Go ) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume. SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove , turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs. Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail. We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest. Validation with openenv validate A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials: The reference solution earns the maximum reward ( semantic.oracle_max ). Doing nothing scores clearly lower ( semantic.floor_gap ). No canary scores more than doing nothing ( semantic.canary_floor ). A replay of the reference gives the same reward ( runtime.episode_determinism ). Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task: openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded. Difficulty check with the base model A valid task can still teach nothing.

item.title: RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only
item.abstract: This week RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B , its first open-weight model. DaisyRose-27B is an agentic coding model from RadixArk, post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning (RL). The model card page states that it used RL only, with no SFT or distillation. It ships under Apache 2.0 as a drop-in replacement for the base model. The main result: Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 rises from 5.6 to 12.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . DaisyRose-27B keeps the Qwen3.8-27B architecture unchanged. The model card lists 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 pattern. Three Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers alternate with 1 full-attention layer. Hidden size is 5,120. A 27-layer vision encoder handles images. One multi-token-prediction layer supports speculative decoding. Input is text and images, output is text, and it is a thinking model. RadixArk built about 1,200 curated tasks with Eigent AI , chosen from thousands of candidates. Each task targets a specific failure of the base model. Each sandbox attempt allows up to 1.5 hours, 100+ tool calls and 256k+ output tokens. Agent sessions reach up to 1M tokens, per the blog . Training ran on Miles , RadixArk’s open-source RL framework, in fully asynchronous mode. The run used 144 H200 GPUs for 18 days. Of those, 128 handled agent inference and 16 handled training. Total compute was 63,000 GPU-hours. RadixArk reports 37% MFU on its internal backend. An open-source Megatron-based trainer reached 16%. End-to-end throughput was 16.8k tokens/s versus 8.3k, a 2.0x speedup. RadixArk says this cut GPU time by 57%. Sandboxes ran on AgentENV . RadixArk reports about 944,000 sandboxes from mid-September to mid-November. Peak concurrency hit 1,566. Creation success was 99% over 9 weeks. RadixArk puts the cost about 80% below popular cloud sandbox providers. All scores are self-reported by RadixArk. DaisyRose scores are the higher of its BF16 and FP8 runs. Source: RadixArk blog and model card . The largest jump is Terminal Bench 4.1, which more than doubles. Coding gains are steady: +4.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and +3.4 on SWE Bench Pro v2. Knowledge gains are small, at +0.4 on HLE and +1.5 on GPQA Diamond. Against larger models, results are mixed. MiMo V2.6 Flash (309B total) leads Terminal Bench 4.1 at 16.1. Inkling 2 Small (594B total) leads DeepSWE at 72.1 and HLE at 44.1. DaisyRose-27B tops RadixArk’s 9-model table only on IFBench. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16 , FP8 , NVFP4 and GGUF . NVFP4 requires a Blackwell GPU. RadixArk recommends SGLang with DSpark speculative decoding. That setup uses the Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark draft model. vLLM also works via vllm serve "RadixArk/DaisyRose-27B" . Suggested thinking-mode sampling is temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 and top_k 20. *From RadixArk’s comparison table , which cites each developer’s reports or leaderboards. SWE Bench Pro v2 figures trace to arXiv 2611.16289 . The last row comes from each model’s own card. Check out the model card , the technical blog and the Miles repo . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
item.abstract: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems , which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems , there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic , Theorem , Axiom Math , and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett , &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5 , a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) , which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro , Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by Clark Barrett. When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall? “The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. But you're never quite sure, did I find all of them [the issues] or is there one more lurking there that my tool can't find?” &Atlas, the first tool of &Truth; it’s “a map of the world’s open-source code, starting with code written in the C programming language.” &Truth builds on Lean , an open-source programming language and proof assistant . The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check. Lean is a language used by frontier models to solve all manner of supremely difficult math problems . For instance, just this week GPT-6.2 Astra produced what Vals believes is “the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem.” Vals added that Anthropic also used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem, a project of 13 million lines. The latest big math news is a report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and he posted the proof in Lean . Example of Lean code; via Lean project website &Truth is building what it calls a “verification machine” on top of the Lean framework, with the ambition of reading code “in any language, proving whether it satisfies precisely stated requirements , and enabling humans to trust it without having to understand every line.” “What Lean does is it just checks that you didn't make a mistake,” explained Barrett. “So you can think of it as a very sophisticated checker for mathematics.” This has implications for model training too. Axiom Math uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training its mathematical reasoning systems, with proof attempts helping improve future models. In an interview with Latent Space in June , Axiom CEO Carina Hong made the point that formal verification — and what Lean enables — isn’t just a defensive measure. “Formal verification, or verified AI, to us it's not just about handling or kicking out the lousiness, the hallucinations, the mistakes. It's about scaling brilliance. It's about super-intelligence.” Axiom develops AxiomProver , an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside AXLE , its toolkit for exploring, validating, and manipulating those proofs. Harmonic’s Aristotle , an “ automated theorem prover ”, uses Lean heavily in its offering. “Inside Aristotle, AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step of them, so a result never rests on the AI being right,” states the company on its website. Given the heightened level of paranoia about cybersecurity these days — some might say in the days leading up to AGI — formal verification systems seem like they’re needed more than ever. And Barrett confirmed that cybersecurity is a key focus for &Truth. “One really powerful use case for our technology is going through all the C code in the world, whether it be open source or closed source, and trying to ensure that it's memory safe. And then if it's not memory safe, we can point to: here's a problem with this piece of code, you need to fix it so that it's safe.” Security is also a focus of Theorem , one of &Truth’s competitors. “Verification is the only defense that holds while adversaries scale,” Theorem states on its homepage. Theorem’s proof-efficiency eval : “KB of machine code verified per hour on our proof-efficiency eval, by model release date, with 95% intervals.” Theorem has also collaborated with Anthropic on this topic, resulting in a blog post entitled “ LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale .” One of the more encouraging notes in the post is that formal verification, although currently token-expensive, is starting to get more token-efficient. On a set of 36 small verification tasks, Anthropic reported that Opus 5.5 reached a 50% solve rate using about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. This trend is expected to continue as more models are “trained on long verification tasks.” Theorem and Anthropic describe “LLM-scaled formal verification” as a promising approach to providing security guarantees at a previously impractical scale. Anthropic diagram: “from code to a machine-checked guarantee”; in this case using Rocq rather than Lean. Lastly, how does formal verification fit into a developer’s workflow? On its website, &Truth states that developers will move from vibe-coding to “veri-coding” — meaning the verification layer is part of the workflow. “If you've got your verification machine connected to your agent, you can still say, ‘hey, I want you to build this,’ said Barrett. “Maybe there's a little bit of work to really nail down with the agent what the specification is of what you want to build. But then the agent can go under the hood, collaborate with the formal [verification] tool, and essentially what you'll see is almost no difference except your code will work the first time.” The idea, then, is that more of the developer’s time will be spent on spec writing and reviewing than on coding or reviewing code. While I was finishing up this article, I came across this tweet by Cognition dev rel Nader Dabit: Whether the term “outcome engineering” sticks or not, he’s onto something in terms of where we are with coding. When you just tell your team of agents what you want and they go ahead and build it, you (the human developer) need a way to check the correctness of what your agents deliver. If companies like &Truth, Harmonic, Theorem and Axiom Math have their way, formal verification could become an increasingly practical way to check those outcomes.

item.title: Decision AI Explained in 5 Minutes
item.abstract: Decision AI Explained in 5 Minutes Learn how decision models work, how they turn LLMs into faster decision-making systems, and how to run open-source alternatives locally. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 20, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Not every AI task needs a large language model (LLM) that generates text. Sometimes, we just need a model to make a quick decision, such as choosing the right tool, classifying a customer complaint, or deciding whether a transaction looks suspicious. This is where Decision AI comes in. With the release of Jev by TypeSafe AI and several open-source alternatives, we now have models specifically designed to make these decisions without generating unnecessary text. In this article, we will learn how Decision AI works, explore open-source models, and run our first decision model locally using llama.cpp . What Is Decision AI? Decision AI is the use of AI to help make decisions. It is a broad field, but a newer generation of decision models focuses on something quite simple: instead of generating text, the model selects from predefined answers and returns probabilities. These models generally support three types of questions: Choice: Select an option, such as billing, sales, or technical support. Score: Rate something on a scale, such as the urgency of a customer complaint. Yes or no: Estimate whether something is true, such as whether an email is spam. For example, imagine a customer sends an email saying, "I was charged twice for my order." We don't need an LLM to write a lengthy explanation. A decision model can simply identify billing as the most appropriate department and return a probability for that answer. This makes decision models useful for applications that process thousands of similar requests. How Does Decision AI Work? The process is straightforward. We provide the model with some information, define a question, and specify the possible answers. The model evaluates the information and returns its decision with probabilities. Here is a simple workflow: Going back to our customer support example, an illustrative result might look like this: Question Answer Probability Which department? Billing 92% Is it urgent? Yes 81% Does it need human review? No 76% These are hypothetical results. In practice, we would test the model's accuracy and probabilities on real customer messages before automating anything. The main advantage is that the answers are structured, so our application can use them directly without extracting information from generated paragraphs. Turning Large Language Models Into Decision Models We can turn an existing LLM into a decision model by using its internal predictions instead of generating text. When an LLM processes an input, it produces logits , which are raw scores for possible next tokens. We can extract the scores for our predefined answers and apply a mathematical function called softmax to convert them into probabilities. For example, when classifying a product review, the model might produce: Positive: 2.0 (logit) Negative: 1.0 (logit) After applying softmax, we get approximately 73% positive and 27% negative. These probabilities are relative to the options we selected. We can take this further by replacing the usual text-generation layer with a small prediction head and fine-tuning the model on decision-making tasks. This lets it score multiple options, and potentially answer several questions, in a single forward pass. The main advantage is that we skip token-by-token text generation , making repeated decisions faster and more efficient. Open-Source Decision AI Models and Frameworks Jev is a proprietary model available through TypeSafe's API. Although the company has shared some details about its approach, it hasn't published the full architecture, model weights, or training recipe. So we still don't know exactly how everything works under the hood. Meanwhile, the open-source community has been moving incredibly fast, releasing alternatives that we can inspect, fine-tune, and run locally. Some are already reporting better results on specific benchmarks, faster inference, and potentially lower running costs. Here are five projects worth exploring: Laya : A lightweight decision model supporting over 100 languages. It offers fast inference, automatically selects the appropriate model, and runs on modest hardware. Kev : A family of Qwen-based models ranging from 0.8B to 27B parameters. It supports long documents, custom fine-tuning, and deployment through a Jev-compatible API. Simple Jev : Lets us use existing Hugging Face models for classification and scoring without additional training. It also supports vision models for making decisions about images. Decider : Designed to handle multiple decisions in a single forward pass. It supports up to 255 choices per question and includes experimental demonstrations involving games such as Tetris and Pong. SemIf : Focuses on local decision-making, with support for NVIDIA GPUs, Apple Silicon, and CPUs. It includes an interactive browser demo and reproducible benchmarks for comparing accuracy and inference speed. The interesting part is that we now have several ways to build decision-making applications without depending on a closed-source API. We can choose smaller models for speed, fine-tune them for our specific tasks, or run everything locally to reduce API costs. Running Decision AI Locally With llama.cpp Things are moving quickly. Both Ollama and llama.cpp now support decision models through the TypeSafe-compatible /v1/systemone endpoint. Ollama supports models such as Nimble and Tev1, while llama.cpp supports Laya, Kev, Julia-1, and OpenJev. Let's try Laya using the latest llama.cpp. Start the local server: llama update llama serve -hf ggml-org/Laya-GGUF Once the model is running, open another terminal and send a customer support request: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "state": "I was charged twice for my order.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "shipping": "Delivery problems", "technical": "Bugs and account issues" } } } }' The model will evaluate the message and return the selected department along with a probability for each option. That's it. We can now experiment with a decision model locally without using a paid API. The Future of Decision AI I think the most interesting part of Decision AI is how it can work alongside existing LLMs to make AI applications faster and cheaper. Imagine an AI coding agent using a small decision model to select the right tool, decide whether to search the web, or determine if a task needs a more powerful LLM. Instead of using an expensive reasoning model for every little decision, we can reserve it for tasks that actually need it. Another exciting area is real-time applications. Decision models are already being tested in games, where they can choose the next move in milliseconds. We could see similar applications in robotics, fraud detection, and autonomous AI agents. With Ollama and llama.cpp now supporting these models, we can also run them locally, reducing API costs and keeping sensitive data on our own hardware. The biggest challenge is reliability. If a model says it is 95% confident, we need to know whether we can trust that number. Better training, calibration, and human review will be important as these models move into real-world applications. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies. Abid holds a Master's degree in technology management and a bachelor's degree in telecommunication engineering.

item.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
item.abstract: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook  and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is. This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt. We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built. The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams. We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code! The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

item.title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
item.abstract: This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline. Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs. Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar. “At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.” — Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases. Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting. Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria. With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them. The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight. Delivery teams no longer fill it in from scratch. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case’s code repository and documentation. It maps relevant files to each question and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The delivery team then reviews those answers, corrects any mistakes, and adds the evidence the agent couldn’t find. The pipeline works from four kinds of evidence. For documents and code, the pipeline checks whether each artifact contains what its mapped control requires. Each control comes from an international AI standard or framework, or from Standard Bank Group’s own policies. An incident procedure, for example, needs to describe how incidents are reported. For live testing, the pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API. The delivery team supplies questions a typical user would ask. The pipeline adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, which the application is expected to decline. It also sends the same prompt several times, in its original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that the answers stay consistent in meaning. Where the team provides expected answers, the pipeline measures how closely the responses match them. Every response is stored in Amazon S3, so reviewers can see exactly what the application generated. In this step, a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock acts as the judge. The assessment uses the model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization. (Model availability varies by AWS Region, so check the supported models by Region before you deploy.) For each question, the model checks whether specific evidence appears in the artifacts and in the application’s responses, and returns yes or no. Every check maps to a control in an international standard or framework for AI management, AI risk, or AI security. Standard Bank Group also customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. The checks cover the eight AWS responsible AI dimensions in the following table: Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn’t find, and a fixed severity level that the bank’s risk team can adjust. Together they produce a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from. A risk officer can then trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. Figure 2 follows one missing piece of evidence through this process, from the evidence request to the recommended fix. Figure 2: How one finding is traced from evidence to fix Standard Bank Group protects and checks the assessment’s output in two ways. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, ensuring alignment with the bank’s established security and responsible AI standards. The assessment’s model calls pass through the same safeguards the bank enforces across its AWS accounts for its AI workloads. These guardrails screen for harmful content and for attempts to manipulate the model. The assessment is also designed so its output can be checked. Instead of asking the model for an open-ended opinion, the pipeline asks narrow yes-or-no questions, each worded to match a specific control. A fixed formula that the risk team can inspect turns those answers into scores. Each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are and any inconsistent findings are flagged in the review interface. Every judgment is stored with the evidence behind it so that reviewers and auditors can trace how it was reached. The pipeline summarizes the results in a standard format and delivers them as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time.

item.title: Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: Kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models. Previously, using Kimi Code with models on Amazon Bedrock meant configuring a generic connection “provider” with an Amazon Bedrock API key. For many AWS customers, this meant introducing an extra credential to obtain and protect. With v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI. You can now configure the agent to use your standard AWS credential chain, including named profiles and single sign-on (SSO), instead of creating and managing a separate API key. In this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials. We use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example, which supports streaming, configurable reasoning, image input, and client-side tool calling. Amazon Bedrock provides pay-per-token inference for a range of open and proprietary models from leading providers, available through standard APIs . Processing stays within the AWS data boundary, as detailed in the Data protection section of the User Guide. The model cards detail which APIs and features are supported for each model. In older versions of the Kimi Code CLI, you could connect to Amazon Bedrock through a provider with type = "openai" or type = "openai_responses" . These use the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions or Responses APIs, respectively. This approach required you to set the regional base_url and provide an Amazon Bedrock API key . The key could be short-term or long-term, but it was a separate credential for you to obtain and manage. The native provider changes that setup: AWS recommends short-term credentials over long-term credentials. This new path reduces reliance on manually managed API keys, but it doesn’t change your responsibility to protect AWS credentials and scope permissions appropriately. The native provider handles authentication and request routing in four steps: The CLI then streams the model response and can use the model’s client-side tool-calling support during coding tasks. Authentication, authorization, model access, and network connectivity must all succeed for a request to complete. The ephemeral API keys generated by the provider are valid for up to 12 hours or your AWS session length, whichever is shorter. For this walkthrough, we use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example model, accessed through global cross-Region inference for broadest availability and lowest cost. Review the Amazon Bedrock pricing to understand expected costs before using the model. The following example IAM policy grants the permissions used by this walkthrough, for the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model and global inference profile only. Replace ${AWS_REGION} with your source Region (for example, us-west-2 for US West Oregon) and ${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID} with your 12-digit AWS account ID: The foundation-model ARN without a Region or account ID is intentional and required for global cross-Region routing. The BedrockInvokeKimiK31DefaultProject statement is only required if using the openai_responses protocol, not with the default openai (Chat Completions). Security of your AWS environment is a shared responsibility . Review and grant IAM permissions according to the principle of least privilege , particularly for production environments. Consider using a dedicated IAM role for Kimi Code CLI, separate from your regular AWS activities. After your prerequisites are ready, follow these steps to configure AWS authentication, add the provider and model, and send a test request. There are different ways to authenticate with the AWS CLI , depending on your organization’s setup. With Named profiles , you can configure multiple AWS contexts and switch between them. Whichever approach you choose, your session resolves to an IAM identity (user or role) that needs the Amazon Bedrock permissions from the prerequisites. A Region configured in an AWS CLI profile applies to AWS CLI commands, but you must still set the Region explicitly for Kimi Code in Step 2. Verify that the AWS CLI resolves your intended identity. Omit --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME if you use the default profile: The model alias bedrock-kimi-k3-1 is a local name used by Kimi Code CLI. The model value is the Amazon Bedrock global inference-profile ID. The example declares a 1-million-token context window and explicit reasoning, image-input, and tool-use capabilities. It omits api_key , api_key_env , and AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK , so the provider uses ambient AWS credentials. A configured Amazon Bedrock key would take precedence. Because you set default_model , the session selects bedrock-kimi-k3-1 automatically. Ask the agent to explain the repository or propose a small change. Review its proposed file modifications and shell commands before approving them. At the time of writing, the native bedrock provider has several configuration considerations. These practices help you avoid ambiguous status information and mismatched settings. At the time of writing, Kimi Code’s desktop and web provider-creation interfaces don’t expose all the provider environment fields used by this credential-chain setup. Edit config.toml directly to set up the Amazon Bedrock provider. For further details, refer to Model providers in the Kimi Code documentation. Kimi Code doesn’t auto-detect the capabilities of most models on Amazon Bedrock, including Kimi models. Check the Amazon Bedrock model card for each target model and explicitly declare its capabilities to let Kimi Code make use of them. For example, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports always_thinking , thinking , image_in , and tool_use , but not audio_in or video_in , as reflected in the config.toml example shown earlier. These declarations describe client behavior. You should only include capabilities that are supported for each target model and Amazon Bedrock API endpoint. Validate tool and image workflows for your application rather than relying on the capability labels alone. The bedrock provider requires an explicit AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION in Kimi Code’s config.toml or the shell environment. It can’t infer a Region configured only in ~/.aws/config or through aws configure . When you use cross-Region inference profiles (with prefixes such as global. , us. , or in. ), the configured Kimi Code Region controls the source Region that receives your requests. For more information, refer to cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For workloads without data-residency requirements, start with the global inference profile. This model, like many others, is priced 10% lower for global inference than through geographic profiles. Review Amazon Bedrock pricing for current rates and geographic alternatives. In some cases, the provider’s auto-detection might mistake the API protocol or target URL you want to use for a particular model. For example, you will need to set a different URL to use Amazon Bedrock through a VPC endpoint or the Mantle endpoints . In the Kimi Code config.toml , you can: In the following example, we show a configuration to connect to the same model but using the OpenAI Responses API through an Amazon Bedrock VPC endpoint you’ve set up: In the Kimi Code desktop and web apps, the provider list can show connected for a bedrock provider. That status doesn’t validate the configured AWS credentials, IAM permissions, Region, model access, or network path. Don’t treat it as proof of a successful model request. Use the non-interactive prompt to test the complete path, and diagnose the actual response if it fails. If you created a new AWS IAM identity or assigned new permissions to experiment with Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, remember to delete them when you’re finished testing. You might also want to revert any local Kimi Code CLI provider configurations or AWS CLI profiles you set up. You can even uninstall the CLIs altogether if they’re no longer required.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
item.abstract: From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more launches for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference In September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint. Most of them answered one question: how do I get this model serving quickly and reliably? This post covers the 13 launches that came next, bringing the total for 2026 to 26. Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them. For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway and the Global Inference Gateway deliver the routing and multi-Region work, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts. To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat. Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the launches in each The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console. Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents. Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs , then Inference optimization . Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model. SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio. Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call. The SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks. Developer guide : Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters Many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile. Inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, update, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters. Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI Right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed. Inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set search_recipe to max-concurrency-under-sla and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency ( feasible_max ) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one ( infeasible_min ). The search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters ( concurrency_min , concurrency_max , search_max_iterations , and search_initial_points ) bound the cost and speed up convergence. Blog: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent Engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice shows up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend. The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS , gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following: Answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces. For the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April.

item.abstract: As we previewed on our Know Before You IPO pod , Anthropic set its IPO price at $83 and today $ANT closed at $97.17, up 17% from the offering price ( drifting -5% to $92.60 after the close) . The $81.3B offering overtook SpaceX's June IPO as the largest in history. Dario and Daniela ( Dario’s remarks , Founders’ letter ) used the occasion to say Anthropic would pace training and deployment based on whether it could keep its systems safe and under human control. Their Class F shares carry 50.1% of voting power on most shareholder matters. Expect the lockup expiries to weigh on the stock price as about a trillion dollars of shares free up over the next year, while Anthropic has to keep the world’s top model ... for now . AI News for 11/18/2026–11/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits and 544 accounts on X . Search past issues in the AINews archive . Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under $ANT, priced at $83, and opened 34% higher, putting it near a $2T valuation. Listing: Anthropic rang the Nasdaq opening bell ( @kimmonismus , @yacinelearning ). The official account posted a media-only launch item that drew by far the day's highest engagement ( @AnthropicAI ). Opening trade: $ANT opened at $111.50 , which is $28.50 (34.3%) above the $83 IPO price ( @TheRundownAI , @kimmonismus ). Pre-open indications were up ~32% at ~$110 ( @kimmonismus ). Record raise: The $81.3B raised beats SpaceX's $75B (June) as the largest IPO ever ( @TheRundownAI ). Net proceeds: Expected net proceeds are $104.8B including a concurrent private placement. Fully diluted valuation was ~$2T at the open ( @kimmonismus ). AMD investment: AMD agreed to invest $2.5B in Anthropic alongside the IPO. The same morning, AMD fell after a Hunterbrook report that a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker kept shipping newer AMD firmware ( @kimmonismus , source ). CEO statement: Dario Amodei published IPO remarks with a strong safety commitment (details below) ( @AnthropicAI ). Employee wealth: The average employee could be worth >$40M , per SEC filings and investors ( @kimmonismus ). Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are now worth more than the bottom third of US households, about 45M families ( @SteveRattner ). Personal framing: Dario and Daniela lost their father to a disease that became curable a few years later. Dario cited CRISPR's decades-long path from discovery to treatment. Core thesis: Powerful AI working with humans "could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade." He stressed that only early results exist so far. item.title: Open Source vs. Proprietary LLMs: A Decision Framework for 2026
item.abstract: Open Source vs. Proprietary LLMs: A Decision Framework for 2026 A practical guide to choosing between open-weight and commercial models, built around the four questions that actually determine the right answer for your use case. By Vinod Chugani on November 20, 2026 in Language Models "Should we use an open source or proprietary large language model (LLM)?" The answer in 2026 looks very different from what it did eighteen months ago. The capability gap between the two categories has shrunk considerably. Cost dynamics now favor open models at scale but still tilt toward proprietary APIs for low-volume work and rapid iteration. And the practical factors — data privacy, fine-tuning needs, infrastructure capacity, and regulatory compliance — carry more weight than raw benchmark scores in most real-world decisions. This guide doesn't argue for one category over the other. Both are legitimate, and both are widely deployed in production. The goal is to give data scientists and machine learning engineers a structured framework for making the decision based on what actually matters for their situation, not what generates the most online commentary. The framework boils down to four questions: What does your data sensitivity require? What's your usage volume? How much do you need to customize the model? And what can your team's infrastructure handle? Working through those four questions will resolve the open-vs-proprietary decision for the vast majority of use cases. Understanding the Current Model Families Before we get into the decision framework, here's what each category actually contains in 2026. The Open-Weight Landscape "Open source" in the LLM context usually means open-weight. The model weights are publicly available, but the training data, code, and methodology may not be fully disclosed. Licensing terms vary a lot, and some licenses marketed as open source don't meet the Open Source Initiative's formal definition. Here are the leading open-weight model families in 2026: Meta's Llama 4 family remains the most influential open-weight series. Llama 4 Scout stands out with a 10 million token context window, the first open model to hit that scale, making it a real contender for long-context document analysis. The Llama license (Meta Community License) permits commercial use but includes restrictions worth reading carefully before deployment. DeepSeek has established itself as one of the most capable open-weight providers. DeepSeek V3 and its successors benchmark favorably against GPT-4o class models on reasoning and coding tasks. DeepSeek R1 is specifically built for mathematical and logical reasoning, making it the strongest open-weight pick for tasks involving complex multi-step inference. The MIT license is the most permissive of the major open-weight families. Qwen 3.5 (Alibaba) currently sits at the top of several open-weight leaderboards for overall reasoning and coding. The 235B-A22B mixture-of-experts variant goes toe-to-toe with frontier proprietary models on most standard benchmarks. Apache 2.0 licensing makes it commercially accessible. Qwen 3.5 also leads in multilingual performance, especially for Chinese, Arabic, and other non-English languages. Mistral contributes a range of efficient open-weight models, with Mistral Small variants punching above their weight class. Smaller Mistral models (Mistral 7B and Mistral Small) carry Apache 2.0 licenses. Mistral's French origin gives it particular relevance for organizations operating under European data governance frameworks, and Mistral Small 4 fits well into GDPR-aligned EU deployment scenarios. The Proprietary API Landscape Proprietary models are accessed through managed APIs. No weights are available. The provider handles infrastructure, updates, and scaling. The leading proprietary models in 2026 include the GPT-5 series from OpenAI , Claude models from Anthropic , and Gemini models from Google . Each has distinct strengths. Claude's 200K token context window is a clear advantage for long-document analysis. GPT-5's ecosystem depth (SDKs, integrations, structured output formats, Assistants API) makes it the lowest-friction choice for teams already building on OpenAI tooling. Gemini integrates tightly with Google Cloud and Vertex AI, which benefits organizations already in that ecosystem. Proprietary API pricing in 2026 spans a wide range, from \$0.05 per million input tokens for lightweight models up to \$30 per million for frontier-tier models. The mid-tier most commonly used in production (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, Gemini Flash) runs between \$1.25 and \$3.00 per million input tokens. Output tokens cost two to four times the input rate. One big shift in 2026: LLM API pricing has dropped roughly 80% since early 2023, driven by competition from open-weight models and efficiency improvements. Frontier proprietary models still command a 2–5x price premium over equivalent open-weight models accessed through hosted inference providers. The Performance Reality Before working through the framework, it helps to understand what the capability gap actually looks like so you can gauge how much it matters for your specific use case. The big picture: open-weight models have closed 70–90% of the capability gap against frontier proprietary models as measured by standard benchmarks. On specific task categories like coding, structured data extraction, and mathematical reasoning, the best open-weight models match or sometimes exceed proprietary alternatives. The persistent gaps show up in complex multi-step reasoning (where Claude Opus-class models still lead on benchmarks like GPQA Diamond), instruction-following consistency at scale, and performance in low-resource languages. Here's the practical takeaway: for about 80% of data science use cases (text classification, summarization, structured data extraction, retrieval-augmented generation over internal documents, code generation assistance), well-chosen open-weight models deliver results that are functionally indistinguishable from proprietary APIs. For the remaining 20% — which includes nuanced long-form reasoning, complex agentic chains, or applications where output reliability at the tail end matters a lot — proprietary frontier models still hold a measurable edge. Bottom line: evaluate models on your actual tasks, not on published leaderboard scores for tasks you'll never run in production. Open source vs proprietary LLMs decision framework for 2026 (click to enlarge). The Four-Question Decision Framework Question 1: What Does Your Data Require? This is the question that settles the debate most often, and it has nothing to do with cost or capability. If your use case involves data that cannot legally or contractually leave your environment, open-weight self-hosting isn't just an option. It's a requirement. The categories that trigger this include medical records and clinical notes (HIPAA in the US, similar regulations elsewhere), personal financial information (PII, transaction data, account details), proprietary business data under NDA or confidentiality agreements, government and defense data with classification or sovereignty requirements, and EU personal data under GDPR when the API provider's data processing arrangements don't satisfy your legal team. If you fall into any of these categories, the decision branches straight to open-weight self-hosting or a private cloud deployment. Cost and capability comparisons take a back seat because compliance isn't negotiable. If your data can be sent to a third-party API provider (most general business text, public data, anonymized datasets), move on to Questions 2 through 4. Question 2: What Is Your Usage Volume? The cost math for open-weight vs. proprietary APIs isn't linear. It depends heavily on scale. At low volume (under 1 million tokens per month), proprietary APIs are more cost-effective once you factor in the infrastructure and engineering overhead of running your own models.
