item.title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
item.abstract:
Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been. Except in software engineering, somehow. When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.” Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all. To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills. “There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change. Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you? So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing! Which brings me to my next point: All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea . It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? — Em’s blog 2 , emphasis mine. Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar! ↩︎ I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great! ↩︎

item.title: What Comes After AGI?
item.abstract:
For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature. Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress. The continuum of general intelligence To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence , whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum. ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades). Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision. Yet knowing those upper limits doesn’t tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, it’s hard to predict how capable a ‘good enough’ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human. What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both today’s AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted. Cognitive industrialization Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient. Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute , driven by three compounding factors: Hardware manufacturing improvements: Under Moore's law and related trends, compute per dollar has increased by roughly 1.5x per year for six decades - meaning the same investment 18 months from now buys twice the compute. Algorithmic efficiency: The amount of training compute (FLOPs) required to reach a fixed AI performance level has fallen at roughly 3–6x per year over the last decade , while algorithmic efficiency at inference improved by roughly 3x per year. Doubling efficiency is practically equivalent to doubling the stock of physical compute. Compute hardware investment: Spending on AI hardware has grown by roughly 2.5x per year over the past decade. For example, the training compute of the largest frontier training runs grows by more than 4x per year . Multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world. At the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year . A cognitive workload that can be performed by today’s AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023. Extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised . Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services. Is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? It’s certainly not a given , but practical ceilings on compute build-out , and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of today’s AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now. Would cognitive industrialization alone be enough to achieve ASI? If we froze other dimensions of AI progress and only scaled up today’s AIs in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI: there may still be cognitive tasks that AI cannot do without human help. Nonetheless, sheer scale can have a quality of its own . Suppose that we do achieve broadly human-level AI. Then there is clearly a major difference between human-level AIs that are slow and expensive to run, and a world where billions of agents act much faster than humans. That quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself be enough to bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to (weak) ASI. Unlike humans, digital intelligence directly benefits from more and faster compute in several fundamental ways: Processing speed: AI systems can reason, ingest data, and generate outputs at increasingly high rates. Working memory and memorization: Today’s models can literally memorize large parts of the internet and their working memory capacity far exceeds human limits. Substrate independence: The same AI system can migrate from one computer to another, upgrade to faster or more energy-efficient hardware, or run across heterogeneous, spatially distributed fleets. Lossless replication: Digital intelligence can be copied nearly instantly and without loss - not only its source code (akin to DNA), but also its memory state (our lifetime experience). Specialist systems can be trained once, then spawned in millions of copies when needed. High-bandwidth sharing of experiences: Humans must strongly compress experience and knowledge in order to teach others; AIs can replay stored high-bandwidth digital input-output streams across an entire population, and homogeneous AI groups could share raw learning signals directly. Four pathways from AGI to ASI Dramatically more efficient AI and larger compute stocks can scale up the speed and number of AI agents at a given capability level.
